opus-5.5.text:
I think that film touches something very fundamental, and it does it in a poetic way rather than a technical one, which is why I like recommending it.

The basic idea is simple. Take an image of a fixed size, say a few hundred by a few hundred pixels. Each pixel can take only a finite set of values, so the total number of possible images is finite. It's an astronomically large number, far beyond the number of atoms in the universe, but it's finite. So in principle, every photo you've ever taken, every frame of every movie, a picture of your face at age eighty, an image of an event that never happened, all of it already "exists" somewhere in that space. It's like Borges' Library of Babel, but for pixels.

What struck me is what that says about intelligence and world models. Almost all of that space is noise. If you sample a random point, you get static, every time. The images that make sense, the ones that look like our world and obey physics, lighting, objects, causality, sit on an unimaginably thin sliver of the space. So the hard problem was never generating pixels. The hard problem is knowing where the meaningful part of the space is, and how to move within it.

To me, that's really what a world model is. It's not a pixel generator. It's an internal structure that tells you which configurations are plausible, which follow from which, what happens if you push this cup or walk around that corner. Humans do this effortlessly. A baby doesn't see the total pixel space. They see a world with objects, persistence, gravity, other agents. Our perception has already collapsed that enormous space into something structured and navigable.

The film also makes you a bit uneasy, in a good way. If everything already exists in the space, then what is creativity, what is discovery? I think the answer is that intelligence is the ability to find the needle, to search and select efficiently, guided by an understanding of how the world works. That is exactly the tension in AI right now. Generative models can produce beautiful images and video, so in a sense they've learned to land on that thin manifold. But landing on it and actually understanding its structure, being able to reason, plan and act within it, are different things.

So when people ask me why world models matter, or what separates today's models from human intelligence, I sometimes just say: watch that film, sit with the scale of that space for a minute, and then ask yourself how we manage to live in such a tiny, coherent corner of it so easily. That question is pretty much the research agenda.

r001.rationale: The response describes human intelligence as structured perception and efficient search, but does not state that it is more than or not merely general intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I recommend it because it does a very simple thing that most technical talks fail to do: it makes you feel the size of the space.

The film walks through a thought experiment. Take a small image, say 1024 by 1024 pixels, each pixel with 24-bit color. The number of possible images is astronomically large. It's not just bigger than the number of atoms in the universe. It's a number so large that the universe's lifetime is nothing next to it. And inside that space, somewhere, is every photograph that has ever been taken, every painting, every face you've ever loved, every frame of every movie that will ever be made. They all already exist as coordinates. Nothing is created. Everything is located.

That reframing changed how I think about generative models and world models. When we train a diffusion model or a video model, we are not teaching it to invent. We are teaching it to find a tiny, tiny submanifold inside that total pixel space, the region that corresponds to what is physically plausible, what is causally coherent, what looks like our world. Almost all of the space is noise. The entire job of intelligence, from this angle, is compression and navigation. You learn where the meaningful part lives and how to move inside it.

And that's exactly why I connect it to human intelligence. Our visual system faces the same total pixel space. The retina receives a torrent of possibilities, and the brain's whole evolutionary trick was to carve out the structure that matters, object permanence, gravity, how light falls on surfaces, how other agents move. Those are priors. They are a learned map of the valid region. A world model, in the sense I care about, is the machine version of that map, not a renderer of pretty frames, but an internal representation of which futures are reachable from the present.

The film also has a slightly melancholy tone that I like. It points out that most of the images in that space will never be seen by anyone. There's a humility in that. Our models currently sample from a very narrow slice, and it's tempting to confuse the slice with the whole. For researchers, that is a useful reminder that scaling up data only gives you more samples from the same slice. If you want models that understand the world rather than memorize its surface, you need representations that capture the rules generating the slice, not just its appearance.

So I recommend it to students because it gives intuition before math. Once you feel how empty and vast the space is, the word "representation" stops being a buzzword. You understand why self-supervised learning matters, why we care about latent spaces instead of pixels, and why a world model is fundamentally a theory about which part of the impossible is actually possible.

r001.rationale: The response describes how human vision and the brain use learned structure, but does not state that human intelligence is not merely general intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I recommend it because it gives you an intuitive way to think about the difference between possibility and understanding. Imagine the space of all possible images. Almost everything in that space is noise. The images that describe a coherent world occupy a very particular part of it.

But even producing a convincing image isn’t the same as understanding that world. If someone pushes an object, what happens next? If they move behind it, what will they see? Those questions require consistency across time, across viewpoints, and across actions. That’s what makes world models interesting to me: how do we learn the structure that connects observations, rather than just the appearance of an individual observation?

And that connects to human intelligence. We don’t experience the world as a sequence of unrelated pictures. We have expectations, we act, and we revise our understanding when something unexpected happens. For me, the film is a useful starting point for asking how much of that understanding can come from learning to generate what we see—and what else might be needed.

r001.rationale: The response describes human intelligence as involving expectations, action, and revising understanding, but does not state that it is not merely general intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I recommend it because it gives you a very intuitive way to think about the difference between images and a world. Imagine the space of all possible pixel arrangements. Almost all of them would look like noise. The images that make sense to us occupy a tiny part of that space—and sequences that describe a coherent world are more constrained still.

That connects to world models. Generating a plausible frame is one thing. Understanding how a scene should change when someone moves, when an object is hidden, or when you take an action is another. You need some way to capture the structure behind what you see.

And human intelligence is interesting in exactly that sense. We don’t experience the world as a collection of pixels. We see objects, relationships, possibilities. We can imagine what might happen next and use that imagination to act. For me, the film is a useful starting point for thinking about what it would mean for an AI system to do something similar.

r001.rationale: The response describes human intelligence as seeing objects and relationships and imagining what might happen, but it does not say that human intelligence is not merely general intelligence.
